label: Justice
definition_short: Harmonic order and right function of the soul; the integrating virtue by which the soul achieves unity and proper relationship among its faculties, and thus participates in the universal order of the cosmos.
definition_long:
Justice, or dikaiosyne in Greek, represents in Neoplatonic philosophy the virtue of harmony and right order, both within the individual soul and in the cosmos at large. Justice is not merely a matter of fair dealing in external transactions, though it encompasses this; it is fundamentally the principle by which the soul achieves unity and integration among its multiple faculties and dimensions. The just soul is one in which reason rules appropriately, in which the spirited and passionate parts function in proper subordination to reason, and in which all faculties work together toward the soul's genuine good. Beyond the individual soul, justice extends to the universal order: the cosmos itself is characterized by justice insofar as each being and level of reality maintains its proper place and function within the vast hierarchy of existence.

In Plotinian metaphysics, justice operates at multiple levels corresponding to the hierarchical structure of reality and virtue. At the civic or social level, justice involves the fair and appropriate conduct of the embodied soul within human society: honoring contracts, treating others with equity, giving to each their due. This civic justice maintains social stability and is valuable and necessary for the embodied life. However, it remains oriented primarily toward external conduct and social relationships. At the purificatory level, justice undergoes a profound transformation. The purificatorily just soul is one that has brought its own faculties into right order, that has established the rational and higher dimensions of the soul in their rightful dominion over the passionate and bodily parts. This internal justice is far more fundamental and consequential than external justice, for it represents the soul's achievement of its own authentic being and harmony.

The key to understanding Neoplatonic justice is recognizing that justice is not primarily a matter of external fairness or conformity to laws, but rather the soul's achievement of internal unity and right function. When all parts of the soul are properly ordered and functioning according to their nature, when reason guides without tyranny, when the spirited element supports reason without rebellion, when the appetitive part serves the higher functions without domination, then the soul is just. This internal justice is experienced as a profound harmony and peace, for the constant internal conflict that characterizes the unordered soul has been resolved. All that was scattered, fragmented, and at war with itself becomes integrated into a coherent whole directed toward its true good.

Plotinus emphasizes that this internal justice naturally gives rise to right external conduct, but the reverse is not necessarily true. A person may conduct themselves fairly and equitably in external dealings while remaining internally disordered. Such external justice, divorced from internal harmony, lacks genuine virtue because it does not reflect the soul's authentic orientation toward the good. True justice must begin from within, from the achievement of the soul's own right order and harmony. Once this internal justice is established, the just soul naturally conducts itself appropriately toward others, not from adherence to external rules but from the inner principle of rightness that characterizes its being.

The relationship between justice and the other virtues deserves careful attention. Justice is sometimes described as the integrating virtue—the virtue that binds the other virtues together and ensures their proper functioning. Wisdom guides the soul toward the eternal and intelligible; courage sustains it through difficulty; temperance frees it from material domination; but justice is what ensures that these virtues function as an integrated whole directed toward authentic flourishing. Justice establishes the proper relationship among the virtues themselves, ensuring that each operates appropriately at each level and that all work together toward the soul's ultimate good. In this sense, the just soul is the virtuous soul in the fullest sense, for in it all virtues have achieved their perfection and integration.

At the contemplative level, justice manifests as the soul's right alignment with the intelligible realities it contemplates. The contemplatively just soul does not introduce distortion or personal desire into its knowledge of eternal truths; rather, it opens itself transparently to what is, allowing the intelligible realities to impress themselves upon consciousness without interference from ego-bound perspective. This justice is a kind of perfect truthfulness, an openness to reality as it is. At the paradigmatic level, which exists eternally in the Divine Intellect, justice represents the infinite harmony and perfect order of the intelligible realm itself, the seamless rightness with which each intelligible form relates to every other and to the infinite whole.

Justice also extends cosmologically. The cosmos itself is characterized by justice insofar as it maintains perfect order and hierarchy. Each level of being functions according to its nature; each creature fulfills its role in the larger whole; all parts work together in the vast symphony of existence orchestrated by the World Soul's eternal contemplation of the Divine Intellect. This cosmic justice is not imposed from without but is the natural expression of the World Soul's eternal intelligence and the overflow of the Divine Intellect. The material realm, though lowest in ontological rank and characterized by greater privation and disorder than higher realms, still participates in cosmic justice insofar as it maintains whatever order and beauty it does manifest.

Plotinus discusses at length how justice binds society together and makes communal life possible. Social order depends on members of the community being ordered within themselves. When souls within a society are just—internally ordered and aligned toward the common good—they naturally form stable and harmonious communities. When souls are internally disordered—dominated by unbridled passions and selfish desires—they inevitably disrupt social harmony regardless of external laws or enforcement. This understanding suggests that the true foundation of justice in society is the internal justice of its members. Laws and external structures are necessary supports for those not yet internally just, but the ideal society would be one whose members had achieved such internal justice that they needed no external compulsion.

The historical development of justice within the Neoplatonic tradition shows consistent emphasis on its nature as internal harmony and its status as the integrating virtue. Plotinus, drawing on Platonic foundations, develops a comprehensive doctrine of justice at multiple levels. Porphyry elaborates on the different manifestations of justice at civic, purificatory, contemplative, and paradigmatic levels. Iamblichus emphasizes justice as essential to the proper functioning of the individual soul and society. Later Neoplatonists, particularly Proclus, integrate justice into systematic metaphysical accounts of universal order and hierarchy.

The transmission of Neoplatonic justice to subsequent philosophical and theological traditions proved profoundly influential. Christian theology, particularly through thinkers influenced by Pseudo-Dionysius and Neoplatonism, integrated Neoplatonic justice into theological virtue theory, treating justice as both a human virtue and a divine attribute. Medieval Christian philosophy made justice central to natural law theory and ethics. Islamic philosophy incorporated Neoplatonic justice into theological and ethical thought. Renaissance Neoplatonists recovered Plotinian justice as central to their vision of both individual virtue and social order. Modern political philosophy, despite often departing from metaphysical frameworks, continues to grapple with questions about the relationship between internal virtue and external justice that Neoplatonism posed.

Justice illuminates profound truths about the soul, the cosmos, and human flourishing. First, it demonstrates that authentic justice must be rooted in the soul's internal harmony and right order, not merely in external conformity or adherence to rules. Second, it shows that the individual soul is not isolated but participates in larger orders—the universal order of the cosmos, the order of human community—and finds its greatest good in right alignment with these larger wholes. Third, it establishes that virtue and happiness are inseparable: the just soul, precisely because it has achieved internal harmony and right order, experiences profound peace and fulfillment. Fourth, it suggests that social order and justice must be grounded in the transformation of individual souls, not merely in external structures and enforcement.

In contemporary philosophy and social thought, Neoplatonic justice offers challenging resources. It suggests that mere external fairness and conformity to law, without internal transformation and alignment with what is truly good, is insufficient. It proposes that genuine social justice depends on the development of virtuous souls within the society. It challenges the separation of individual virtue from social justice, suggesting instead that they are intimately connected. For those who engage authentically with Neoplatonic philosophy, justice becomes not merely a social or legal concept but a comprehensive principle of harmony and right order—in the soul, in society, and in the cosmos itself.

sections.opening_definition: Justice is the virtue of harmony and right order both within the soul and in the cosmos; the integrating principle by which all faculties achieve proper function and relationship, and by which the individual soul aligns itself with the universal order of reality.
sections.historical_usage: In classical Greek thought, dikaiosyne denoted fairness, righteousness, and right conduct. Plato developed justice as the cardinal virtue of the soul's internal harmony and order. Neoplatonism inherited and elaborated this understanding, treating justice as the principle of integration and right function at every level of reality.
sections.philosophical_significance: Justice demonstrates that authentic virtue must be rooted in internal harmony and right order of the soul's faculties. It shows that the individual participates in larger universal orders and finds genuine good through right alignment with them. It establishes that social justice depends on the virtue of individual souls. It suggests that happiness and virtue are inseparable.
sections.development_across_schools: Plotinus developed a comprehensive doctrine of justice at multiple levels of the soul and reality. Porphyry elaborated on civic, purificatory, contemplative, and paradigmatic manifestations of justice. Iamblichus emphasized justice as essential to individual and social functioning. Proclus integrated justice into systematic metaphysics of universal order.
sections.transmission: Christian theology integrated Neoplatonic justice into virtue theory and natural law doctrine. Medieval philosophy made justice central to ethics and social order. Islamic thought incorporated Neoplatonic principles of justice. Renaissance Neoplatonists recovered justice as central to virtue and social philosophy. Modern political philosophy continues to engage with Neoplatonic insights on justice.
